# Expert Question 1 — Defining "lasts longest": structural collapse vs. geometric survival

## Problem Understanding

**Current interpretation.** MCM 2020 Problem B asks for the 3-D foundation shape of a
wet-sand castle that (1) lasts longest on a beach with waves and tides,
(2) pairs with the optimal sand-to-water proportion, and (3) is re-examined
under rain, plus (4) other longevity strategies and (5) a non-technical article.
All candidates are constrained to equal sand volume, same sand type, same
distance from water, same water/sand proportion, so shape is the only
geometric degree of freedom.

**Modeling objective / current stage.** Before committing to the erosion
sub-model I need to fix the definition of "lasts longest." I will model survival
as a two-layer quantity: (i) the foundation's *integrity* — its resistance to
structural failure (shear sliding, capillary-driven mass loss, wet-out), and
(ii) its *geometric presence* — remaining volume above the lowest wave wash
level. Two natural candidate definitions differ sharply in the shape they
reward:

## Decision Point

**Which survival metric should define "lasts longest"?**

- **Option A — Last-to-collaps (structural failure first).** Survival time =
  time until the foundation's structural integrity fails (sliding/erosion
  outpaces capillary cohesion). Wave impact and swash wet-out drive the
  failure. A shape with large mass below the wash line survives longer even
  if its upper part is trimmed away.
- **Option B — Last-recognizable (geometry-first).** Survival time = time
  until the shape can no longer be read as its intended form (e.g., less
  than 50% of initial cross-section at each elevation remains, or the
  centroid of remaining mass drops below the original half-height). A tall,
  slim shape that holds its silhouette outlasts a squat one under this rule.

**Why it matters.** The two metrics favor opposite extremes: A rewards
low-slung, high-mass shapes (e.g., a low cylinder or squat hemisphere) that
bury most sand below the wash; B rewards shapes with a high center of mass
and small wave-exposed perimeter (e.g., a tall cone or tapered tower). The
shape ranking, and hence the whole Requirement 1, pivots on this choice. The
mixture optimum (~1% liquid by volume, Pakpour 2012) and the rain analysis
(Requirement 3) are downstream and will be developed once the shape question
is settled.

## Candidate Strategies

**Option A (structural failure clock).**
- Approach: track a scalar integrity I(t) from a capillary-cohesion balance
  against wave/splash erosion and tidal wetting; survival = first t with I = 0.
- Advantages: physically grounded; directly uses the capillary-bridge strength
  peak from Pakpour et al. (2012); clean two-parameter model (shape enters
  only through wetted perimeter and exposed face area).
- Limitations: says nothing about whether the castle still *looks* like a
  castle; a shape can be "alive" but unrecognizable.
- Expected impact: favors low, mass-consolidated shapes.

**Option B (geometric recognizability clock).**
- Approach: track volume remaining above the lowest wave level per elevation
  slice; survival = first t at which remaining fraction < threshold.
- Advantages: matches the common human notion of "the castle lasted."
- Limitations: the threshold (50%? 30%?) is arbitrary and must be tuned; the
  answer becomes threshold-sensitive rather than physics-sensitive.
- Expected impact: favors tall, slender shapes with small upper-exposed area.

**Option C (composite).** Score = α·(integrity time) + (1−α)·(recognizable time)
with α calibrated so neither dominates. More faithful to the problem's
"recognizable 3-D geometric shape" wording but adds an arbitrary α.

I lean toward **A as the primary metric with B reported as a secondary
sensitivity**, because (i) A is the only option whose numbers come from the
citable capillary-physics anchor already in the data file, (ii) B's threshold
is arbitrary, and (iii) a composite inherits both weaknesses. Please confirm
this choice, or redirect me to B or C as the primary.

# Expert Question 2 — Should the "best shape" be a *pure* geometric solid, or is a
# shape *optimized against the swash line* in scope?

## Context / where we are

Per your round-1 ruling I use the last-to-collapse (structural) metric. I have
built a closed-form erosion + factor-of-safety model and run it over four
recognizable solids, all scaled to the same 0.05 m³ and same ~1% optimum
mixture:

| Shape (V=0.05 m³) | No-rain survival | FS |
|---|---|---|
| Hemisphere (r=0.29 m) | **26 min (best)** | ∞ |
| Cube (s=0.37 m) | 14 min | 2.2 |
| Cone (H=2b, H=0.58 m) | 12 min | 7.3 |
| Cylinder (H=2r, H=0.40 m) | 9.5 min | 1.5 |

The hemisphere wins because it buries essentially all of its volume at or below
the 0.3 m swash line (small wave-exposed band per unit wetted volume, no dry
overburden to lose grip on). Under rain (φ→15%, cohesion 3000→145 Pa, whole
surface exposed) the hemisphere *remains* the only shape with FS>1, so it stays
the best. Ranking is stable across H_s and k_eros; it flips to the cylinder only
at an extreme 0.5 m run-up.

## Decision Point

The problem says the builder "cuts and shapes this base into a *recognizable*
3-dimensional geometric shape." I read the candidate set as **pure,
recognizable solids** (the four above), and the "best" is the hemisphere.

But there is a second, defensible reading: the *foundation* can be any shape
the model deems optimal, in which case the true optimum is a **shape adapted to
the swash line** — e.g., a squat dome / half-capsule that maximizes mass at or
below h_w with the minimum wave-abraded face, i.e. a hemisphere *truncated or
flattened* so its top sits near the run-up level, or a hemisphere fused with a
shallow wide base ("dome on a plinth"). That hybrid is still a recognizable
solid (a truncated dome / half-capsule) and would survive longer than a pure
hemisphere by reducing the exposed upper band further.

**Which scope do you want the headline Recommendation-1 answer to take?**

- **Option 1 — Pure solids only.** The answer is "the hemisphere." Clean,
  directly comparable, and the four-solid comparison *is* the deliverable.
- **Option 2 — Allow a swash-adapted solid.** The answer is "a truncated dome /
  half-capsule whose top lies at or below the run-up line" — the hemisphere is
  its limiting case, and I add the optimized truncated-dome as the true winner.

**Why it matters.** Option 2 makes the model genuinely *optimizing* (the shape
is derived from the swash geometry rather than picked from a menu), which a
strong MCM solution is expected to do; Option 1 keeps it a clean comparative
study. Both use the same physics; the difference is whether I present a
derived optimum or a menu comparison.

## My lean

I lean **Option 2, framed as "the hemisphere is the optimal *pure* solid, and
the model's true optimum is a swash-truncated dome (a flattened hemisphere /
half-capsule) whose crest stays at or below the run-up level"** — i.e., present
the four-solid menu (Option 1) *and* the derived swash-adapted dome as the
final Recommendation-1 shape, showing it out-survives the pure hemisphere. This
gives a defensible pure-solid winner and a genuinely optimized shape in one
coherent answer, without inventing an arbitrary free shape.

Please confirm Option 1, Option 2, or the combined framing.

# Expert Question 3 — How to present the absolute survival time given the
# lumped entrainment coefficient

## Context / where we are

Per your round-1 (last-to-collapse metric) and round-2 (four-solid menu +
derived swash-optimized dome) rulings, the model is built and run. Results:

- **Best pure solid (no rain):** hemisphere, ~26 min; then cube 14, cone 12,
  cylinder 9.5 min.
- **Derived optimum (dome with crest at the run-up line h_w=0.3 m):** a
  spherical cap with R=0.28 m ≈ the hemisphere's a=0.29 m — i.e., for a 0.05 m³
  base and 0.3 m run-up, the swash-optimized dome *coincides with* the
  hemisphere (its crest already sits at the run-up line). So the hemisphere is
  both the best pure solid and the derived optimum.
- **Optimal mixture:** φ* ≈ 1% liquid (sand:water ≈ 99:1 by volume), matching
  Pakpour 2012.
- **Rain (φ→15%):** hemisphere remains the only shape with FS>1 (all others
  collapse immediately when waterlogged), so it stays the best; survival drops
  26 min → ~2.5 min.
- Ranking is stable across H_s (0.5–2 m) and k_eros (10×); flips to cylinder
  only at an extreme 0.5 m run-up.

## Decision Point

The **shape ranking and all physics-driven conclusions are independent of the
absolute clock**, but the *reported survival times* (26 min, 2.5 min, …) depend
on the lumped entrainment efficiency k_eros (and the wave energy-flux), which I
calibrated so the best shape survives ~30 min — a plausible order of magnitude
for a sandcastle on the swash line, but not a measured constant. Two ways to
present the absolute numbers:

- **Option A — Report absolute times with an explicit calibration caveat.**
  State k_eros is calibrated to a ~30-min best-case lifetime (observed
  order-of-magnitude for beach sandcastles) and that the times carry O(10×)
  uncertainty; emphasize the *ratios* (hemisphere ≈ 5× cylinder, ≈ 2× cube) and
  the rain factor (≈10× reduction) as the robust results.
- **Option B — Report only dimensionless ratios / relative survival.**
  Normalize every shape's survival to the hemisphere (=1.0) and present only
  relative longevity (cube 0.53, cone 0.45, cylinder 0.36; rain = 0.1× no-rain),
  avoiding any absolute-minute claim entirely.

**Why it matters.** Option A gives a concrete, intuitive answer ("a dome last
about half an hour before the tide takes it") but leans on the calibration;
Option B is fully defensible and needs no calibration but is less concrete for a
general-audience magazine article (Requirement 5). A judge may prefer the
honesty of B, but the problem and the magazine article both want a tangible
number.

## My lean

I lean **Option A with Option B's ratios reported alongside**: give the absolute
~26-min headline as a *calibrated order-of-magnitude* estimate (clearly labeled
as such, with the 10× band), and lead with the calibration-free ratios and the
rain reduction factor as the robust, defensible core. This gives the magazine a
concrete number while keeping every physics claim independent of the calibration.

Please confirm Option A (+ratios), Option B only, or a different presentation.
expert_answers: Confirm Option A as the primary survival metric, with B reported as a secondary sensitivity. This is the right call: A is anchored in the citable capillary-cohesion physics (Pakpour 2012) already in your data file, so the shape ranking follows from mechanism rather than an arbitrary cutoff. B's threshold is a free parameter that would let you tune the answer, and C inherits that arbitrariness while diluting A's physical grounding. Keep B strictly as a robustness check to show the ranking is not an artifact of the metric choice.

Confirm the combined framing. Present the four-solid menu as the comparative core (hemisphere wins among pure recognizable solids), then derive the swash-truncated dome / half-capsule as the model's true optimum, with the hemisphere as its limiting case. This is the right scope: it keeps the clean, directly comparable menu the problem's "recognizable geometric shape" wording invites, while making the model genuinely optimizing rather than a pick-from-menu exercise — which is what distinguishes a strong solution. The truncated dome is still a recognizable solid, so you avoid inventing an arbitrary free-form shape. One constraint: keep the truncation tied to the swash/run-up geometry you already model, not to a tuned free parameter, so the derived optimum follows from mechanism. Report the pure-hemisphere result as the headline comparable answer and the truncated dome as the refined optimum.

Confirm Option A with the ratios reported alongside. Lead with the calibration-free results — the shape ratios (hemisphere ≈ 2× cube, ≈ 5× cylinder) and the rain reduction factor (≈10×) — as the robust, defensible core, since these are independent of k_eros. Then give the ~26-min absolute headline explicitly labeled as a calibrated order-of-magnitude estimate with an O(10×) band, tied to the observed ~30-min best-case lifetime you used to fix k_eros. This satisfies both audiences: the magazine gets a tangible number, and every physics claim stays independent of the calibration. Do not present the absolute times without the caveat, and do not drop them entirely — the problem and Requirement 5 both want a concrete figure.

# Expert Question 1 — Defining "lasts longest": structural collapse vs. geometric survival

## Problem Understanding

**Current interpretation.** MCM 2020 Problem B asks for the 3-D foundation shape of a
wet-sand castle that (1) lasts longest on a beach with waves and tides,
(2) pairs with the optimal sand-to-water proportion, and (3) is re-examined
under rain, plus (4) other longevity strategies and (5) a non-technical article.
All candidates are constrained to equal sand volume, same sand type, same
distance from water, same water/sand proportion, so shape is the only
geometric degree of freedom.

**Modeling objective / current stage.** Before committing to the erosion
sub-model I need to fix the definition of "lasts longest." I will model survival
as a two-layer quantity: (i) the foundation's *integrity* — its resistance to
structural failure (shear sliding, capillary-driven mass loss, wet-out), and
(ii) its *geometric presence* — remaining volume above the lowest wave wash
level. Two natural candidate definitions differ sharply in the shape they
reward:

## Decision Point

**Which survival metric should define "lasts longest"?**

- **Option A — Last-to-collaps (structural failure first).** Survival time =
  time until the foundation's structural integrity fails (sliding/erosion
  outpaces capillary cohesion). Wave impact and swash wet-out drive the
  failure. A shape with large mass below the wash line survives longer even
  if its upper part is trimmed away.
- **Option B — Last-recognizable (geometry-first).** Survival time = time
  until the shape can no longer be read as its intended form (e.g., less
  than 50% of initial cross-section at each elevation remains, or the
  centroid of remaining mass drops below the original half-height). A tall,
  slim shape that holds its silhouette outlasts a squat one under this rule.

**Why it matters.** The two metrics favor opposite extremes: A rewards
low-slung, high-mass shapes (e.g., a low cylinder or squat hemisphere) that
bury most sand below the wash; B rewards shapes with a high center of mass
and small wave-exposed perimeter (e.g., a tall cone or tapered tower). The
shape ranking, and hence the whole Requirement 1, pivots on this choice. The
mixture optimum (~1% liquid by volume, Pakpour 2012) and the rain analysis
(Requirement 3) are downstream and will be developed once the shape question
is settled.

## Candidate Strategies

**Option A (structural failure clock).**
- Approach: track a scalar integrity I(t) from a capillary-cohesion balance
  against wave/splash erosion and tidal wetting; survival = first t with I = 0.
- Advantages: physically grounded; directly uses the capillary-bridge strength
  peak from Pakpour et al. (2012); clean two-parameter model (shape enters
  only through wetted perimeter and exposed face area).
- Limitations: says nothing about whether the castle still *looks* like a
  castle; a shape can be "alive" but unrecognizable.
- Expected impact: favors low, mass-consolidated shapes.

**Option B (geometric recognizability clock).**
- Approach: track volume remaining above the lowest wave level per elevation
  slice; survival = first t at which remaining fraction < threshold.
- Advantages: matches the common human notion of "the castle lasted."
- Limitations: the threshold (50%? 30%?) is arbitrary and must be tuned; the
  answer becomes threshold-sensitive rather than physics-sensitive.
- Expected impact: favors tall, slender shapes with small upper-exposed area.

**Option C (composite).** Score = α·(integrity time) + (1−α)·(recognizable time)
with α calibrated so neither dominates. More faithful to the problem's
"recognizable 3-D geometric shape" wording but adds an arbitrary α.

I lean toward **A as the primary metric with B reported as a secondary
sensitivity**, because (i) A is the only option whose numbers come from the
citable capillary-physics anchor already in the data file, (ii) B's threshold
is arbitrary, and (iii) a composite inherits both weaknesses. Please confirm
this choice, or redirect me to B or C as the primary.

# Expert Question 2 — Should the "best shape" be a *pure* geometric solid, or is a
# shape *optimized against the swash line* in scope?

## Context / where we are

Per your round-1 ruling I use the last-to-collapse (structural) metric. I have
built a closed-form erosion + factor-of-safety model and run it over four
recognizable solids, all scaled to the same 0.05 m³ and same ~1% optimum
mixture:

| Shape (V=0.05 m³) | No-rain survival | FS |
|---|---|---|
| Hemisphere (r=0.29 m) | **26 min (best)** | ∞ |
| Cube (s=0.37 m) | 14 min | 2.2 |
| Cone (H=2b, H=0.58 m) | 12 min | 7.3 |
| Cylinder (H=2r, H=0.40 m) | 9.5 min | 1.5 |

The hemisphere wins because it buries essentially all of its volume at or below
the 0.3 m swash line (small wave-exposed band per unit wetted volume, no dry
overburden to lose grip on). Under rain (φ→15%, cohesion 3000→145 Pa, whole
surface exposed) the hemisphere *remains* the only shape with FS>1, so it stays
the best. Ranking is stable across H_s and k_eros; it flips to the cylinder only
at an extreme 0.5 m run-up.

## Decision Point

The problem says the builder "cuts and shapes this base into a *recognizable*
3-dimensional geometric shape." I read the candidate set as **pure,
recognizable solids** (the four above), and the "best" is the hemisphere.

But there is a second, defensible reading: the *foundation* can be any shape
the model deems optimal, in which case the true optimum is a **shape adapted to
the swash line** — e.g., a squat dome / half-capsule that maximizes mass at or
below h_w with the minimum wave-abraded face, i.e. a hemisphere *truncated or
flattened* so its top sits near the run-up level, or a hemisphere fused with a
shallow wide base ("dome on a plinth"). That hybrid is still a recognizable
solid (a truncated dome / half-capsule) and would survive longer than a pure
hemisphere by reducing the exposed upper band further.

**Which scope do you want the headline Recommendation-1 answer to take?**

- **Option 1 — Pure solids only.** The answer is "the hemisphere." Clean,
  directly comparable, and the four-solid comparison *is* the deliverable.
- **Option 2 — Allow a swash-adapted solid.** The answer is "a truncated dome /
  half-capsule whose top lies at or below the run-up line" — the hemisphere is
  its limiting case, and I add the optimized truncated-dome as the true winner.

**Why it matters.** Option 2 makes the model genuinely *optimizing* (the shape
is derived from the swash geometry rather than picked from a menu), which a
strong MCM solution is expected to do; Option 1 keeps it a clean comparative
study. Both use the same physics; the difference is whether I present a
derived optimum or a menu comparison.

## My lean

I lean **Option 2, framed as "the hemisphere is the optimal *pure* solid, and
the model's true optimum is a swash-truncated dome (a flattened hemisphere /
half-capsule) whose crest stays at or below the run-up level"** — i.e., present
the four-solid menu (Option 1) *and* the derived swash-adapted dome as the
final Recommendation-1 shape, showing it out-survives the pure hemisphere. This
gives a defensible pure-solid winner and a genuinely optimized shape in one
coherent answer, without inventing an arbitrary free shape.

Please confirm Option 1, Option 2, or the combined framing.

# Expert Question 3 — How to present the absolute survival time given the
# lumped entrainment coefficient

## Context / where we are

Per your round-1 (last-to-collapse metric) and round-2 (four-solid menu +
derived swash-optimized dome) rulings, the model is built and run. Results:

- **Best pure solid (no rain):** hemisphere, ~26 min; then cube 14, cone 12,
  cylinder 9.5 min.
- **Derived optimum (dome with crest at the run-up line h_w=0.3 m):** a
  spherical cap with R=0.28 m ≈ the hemisphere's a=0.29 m — i.e., for a 0.05 m³
  base and 0.3 m run-up, the swash-optimized dome *coincides with* the
  hemisphere (its crest already sits at the run-up line). So the hemisphere is
  both the best pure solid and the derived optimum.
- **Optimal mixture:** φ* ≈ 1% liquid (sand:water ≈ 99:1 by volume), matching
  Pakpour 2012.
- **Rain (φ→15%):** hemisphere remains the only shape with FS>1 (all others
  collapse immediately when waterlogged), so it stays the best; survival drops
  26 min → ~2.5 min.
- Ranking is stable across H_s (0.5–2 m) and k_eros (10×); flips to cylinder
  only at an extreme 0.5 m run-up.

## Decision Point

The **shape ranking and all physics-driven conclusions are independent of the
absolute clock**, but the *reported survival times* (26 min, 2.5 min, …) depend
on the lumped entrainment efficiency k_eros (and the wave energy-flux), which I
calibrated so the best shape survives ~30 min — a plausible order of magnitude
for a sandcastle on the swash line, but not a measured constant. Two ways to
present the absolute numbers:

- **Option A — Report absolute times with an explicit calibration caveat.**
  State k_eros is calibrated to a ~30-min best-case lifetime (observed
  order-of-magnitude for beach sandcastles) and that the times carry O(10×)
  uncertainty; emphasize the *ratios* (hemisphere ≈ 5× cylinder, ≈ 2× cube) and
  the rain factor (≈10× reduction) as the robust results.
- **Option B — Report only dimensionless ratios / relative survival.**
  Normalize every shape's survival to the hemisphere (=1.0) and present only
  relative longevity (cube 0.53, cone 0.45, cylinder 0.36; rain = 0.1× no-rain),
  avoiding any absolute-minute claim entirely.

**Why it matters.** Option A gives a concrete, intuitive answer ("a dome last
about half an hour before the tide takes it") but leans on the calibration;
Option B is fully defensible and needs no calibration but is less concrete for a
general-audience magazine article (Requirement 5). A judge may prefer the
honesty of B, but the problem and the magazine article both want a tangible
number.

## My lean

I lean **Option A with Option B's ratios reported alongside**: give the absolute
~26-min headline as a *calibrated order-of-magnitude* estimate (clearly labeled
as such, with the 10× band), and lead with the calibration-free ratios and the
rain reduction factor as the robust, defensible core. This gives the magazine a
concrete number while keeping every physics claim independent of the calibration.

Please confirm Option A (+ratios), Option B only, or a different presentation.

# Expert Question 1 — Scope of the teamwork model: which network scale and outcome target should anchor the analysis?

## Problem understanding

The 2020 MCM problem asks us (as "Intrepid Champion Modeling") to analyze last
season of a soccer team, the Huskies (38 matches, 19 opponents, 23,429 recorded
passes, 59,271 game events, 30 Huskies players). Four sub-questions:
(1) build passing networks and identify patterns from micro (dyads/triads) to
macro (whole network) scale and from minute-to-minute to season length;
(2) identify teamwork performance indicators *beyond points/wins* (diversity of
plays, coordination, distribution of contributions, tempo, etc.) and use them to
build a model of structural, configurational and dynamical teamwork, clarifying
whether strategies work universally or only against certain counter-strategies;
(3) advise the coach on structural strategies to change next season;
(4) generalize to how to design effective teams in society.

The literature we must apply (Buldú, Ferrer & Pastor-Satorras 2018, Front.
Psychol.) gives us: (a) small-world + heavy-tailed degree baseline for passing
networks, tested against null models; (b) betweenness/centrality and centroid
metrics correlate with win probability — so indicators must be validated against
match outcome.

## Decision point

There is one strategic fork that determines most of the downstream work — **which
network and which outcome anchor the core "teamwork model" of sub-question 2**:

- **Option A — Intra-team Huskies network + win/tie/loss:** build the directed
  weighted passing network *among the 30 Huskies players only* (their
  own-to-own passes) and test network indicators (clustering, path length,
  degree distribution, betweenness, centroid, triad census, pass-type entropy)
  against the 3-class match Outcome and goal difference. This is the
  most direct reading of "teamwork" — cooperation between teammates that produces
  success — and it uses the full 38-match outcome distribution.
- **Option B — Match joint network + goal margin:** build a joint Huskies+opponent
  network per match and relate it to the scoreline. Richer (captures interactions
  across teams) but mixes two different organizational units into one graph and
  makes "teamwork" less interpretable; the outcome target collapses to a single
  continuous margin per match.
- **Option C — Opponent-conditioned analysis only:** treat each opponent as a
  regime and build separate models per opponent. This directly answers
  "universally effective or counter-strategy-dependent" but fragments the sample
  (2 matches per opponent, n=38 total) to a point where most statistics are
  underpowered.

My inclination is **A as the primary model, with C as a secondary
robustness/context layer** (opponent-conditioned contrasts of the same
indicators, plus home/away and half-level splits), and B used only for a limited
purpose (e.g., measuring how often passes enter opponent territory via crosses
and forward progress, rather than modeling a joint graph).

## Why it matters

The choice fixes: which indicators enter the core model; what "validation"
means (3-class outcome vs. margin); how we use the small sample (n=38 matches);
and what the coach's actionable advice (sub-3) can legitimately claim. Getting
this wrong risks either an underpowered analysis or a model whose target is not
actually "teamwork."

## Candidate strategies

**Option A — Huskies-only intra-team network, outcome-validated.**
- Approach: aggregate Huskies→Huskies passes per match (and season), build
  dyad/triad census, null-model comparisons (Erdős–Rényi + degree-preserving
  Configuration Model + spatial null), centrality and entropy indicators, then
  correlate with Outcome/gd via effect sizes and a simple regularized classifier.
- Advantages: cleanest "teamwork" semantics; all 38 matches usable; indicators
  directly actionable for the coach; matches the literature baseline.
- Limitations: ignores opponent structure; with n=38 any per-opponent split is
  weak; 30 players → some players appear only in few matches (lineup changes).
- Expected impact: primary model + validation story for sub-questions 2–3.

**Option B — Joint match network.**
- Approach: nodes = all players in the match (10–22), edges = all recorded
  passes; model goal margin from joint network statistics.
- Advantages: captures cross-team interaction and transition passes.
- Limitations: mixes two teams' organization; "teamwork" indicator becomes
  muddled; opponent lineups vary, so the graph structure is driven partly by
  opponent identity rather than Huskies play.
- Expected impact: could be a secondary lens (territory/progress), but risky as
  the core model.

**Option C — Opponent-conditioned only.**
- Approach: separate indicators per opponent and per Side.
- Advantages: directly tests counter-strategy dependence.
- Limitations: n=2 matches per opponent → most contrasts are anecdotal;
  multiplicity across 19 opponents; cannot build a stable core model.
- Expected impact: useful only as a robustness/context layer, not the anchor.

**My recommended synthesis:** Option A anchors the core model; Option C runs as
an opponent/home–away/period conditioning layer on the *same* indicators; Option
B is reduced to territory/progress measures (e.g., x-progress of passes, share of
passes into the final third, crosses) used as supplementary indicators rather
than a joint graph.

## Question

Do you agree that the Huskies-only intra-team passing network, validated
against the 3-class match Outcome (with goal-difference as a secondary
continuous target), should anchor the core teamwork model — with
opponent/home–away/half-conditioned contrasts as a secondary robustness layer,
and joint match-graph analysis reduced to territory/progress measures? Or do you
prefer a different anchor (e.g., margin-anchored joint network), and if so, what
specific change to the anchor and to the validation target would you direct?

# Expert Question 2 — How to handle the (negative) small-world null-model result and the n=38 outcome validation

## Context from round 1

Per your direction, I anchored the core model on the Huskies-only intra-team
directed weighted passing network, validated against the 3-class Outcome (with
goal difference as secondary target), and reduced the joint graph to
territory/progress measures. I have now computed the season-level network
(n=30 players, 656 directed edges, aggregated over all 38 matches) and the
per-match feature table (38 rows).

## Empirical result that forces a strategic decision

The literature baseline (Buldú et al. 2018) says passing networks are
small-world: clustering well above the ER null, path length comparable to ER.
But my computed numbers do **not** show a clean small-world signature at the
season level:

| metric | Huskies real | ER null (n=30, m=656, mean of 50) | Degree-preserving CM null |
|---|---|---|---|
| average clustering | 0.888 | **0.937** | 0.904 |
| average path length | 1.214 | 1.063 | — |

Two issues:
1. With only 30 nodes and a dense graph (edge probability p≈0.74 in the ER null),
   the ER null is itself near-saturated, so its clustering is already ~0.94. The
   real network's clustering (0.888) is *slightly below* both nulls, and its path
   length (1.214) is *above* the ER null (1.063). So the standard "small-world"
   claim (clustering ≫ ER, APL ≈ ER) does **not** hold at season level — the
   network is dense and well-connected but not a clustering outlier.
2. At per-match level the graphs are sparser (~100 edges each), where the
   small-world comparison against a matched ER null is more meaningful, but
   still the absolute clustering is high and APL is short.

So there is a genuine tension: the external literature says "small-world," but
the data, with a properly matched (dense) null, does not show a clustering
outlier. The degree distribution also is not strongly heavy-tailed (out-degree
Gini ≈ 0.15, top hub M11 has betweenness 0.232 but most players have 25–30
out-links), and modularity is very low (0.068), i.e. weak community/formation
structure.

## Decision point

How should I frame and use the small-world / structural claim given that the
matched null-model result is *null* (not a significant outlier), and given the
constrained sample (n=38 matches, 3-class outcome with 13 win / 10 tie / 15 loss)?

- **Option A — Report the null honestly and re-anchor "success" on outcome-correlated indicators.**
  Present the null-model comparison accurately (clustering not an outlier, APL
  slightly longer than ER), conclude the season network is "dense and
  well-connected, hub-lite, weakly modular" rather than "small-world," and then
  lean on the per-match indicators that actually discriminate outcome
  (centroid_x, progress, betweenness balance, pass-type entropy, triad
  completion) for the coach-facing recommendations. This is statistically
  honest but drops the literature's small-world narrative.
- **Option B — Keep the small-world framing but move the comparison to the
  per-match / half scale where the matched null is less saturated.**
  Compute the small-world comparison (clustering vs. ER null, APL vs. ER null)
  *per match* (and per half), where the ER null is less near-saturated, report
  that the signature appears at the match scale (even if averaged out at season
  scale), and treat season-level as an aggregation that dilutes the signal.
  This preserves the literature narrative but risks over-claiming from a
  less-saturated null.
- **Option C — Hybrid: report both scales honestly, and use the outcome
  association (not the null-model novelty) as the main "what makes teamwork
  successful" evidence.** State clearly that the structural baseline is
  "dense, short-path, low-hub, weakly modular" (a small-world-adjacent regime
  but not a clustering outlier vs. matched null), and that the actionable
  insights come from which structural/territorial indicators correlate with
  wins vs. losses — with appropriate caution for n=38 and a 3-way outcome.

## Why it matters

The coach-facing recommendations (sub-3) and the generalized-team design
claims (sub-4) rest on which structural story I tell. If I over-claim
"small-world" the judge (who applied the literature) may credit the
narrative but I risk a statistical over-claim; if I drop it entirely I risk
not applying the provided external finding as instructed. The honest hybrid
(C) applies the literature as a *baseline to test against* (which is exactly
its intended use per external_data.md) while letting the data speak.

## Question

Given the matched-null result shows the season network is **not** a clustering
outlier (real 0.888 vs ER 0.937, CM 0.904) and is only weakly hub-dominated and
weakly modular, which framing do you direct for the submission:
(A) honest "not small-world, dense/well-connected" with success anchored purely
on outcome-correlated indicators;
(B) preserve the small-world narrative by moving the null-model comparison to
per-match / per-half scale;
or (C) the hybrid — report the baseline honestly as "dense, short-path,
low-hub, weakly modular (small-world-adjacent but not a clustering outlier vs
matched null)," apply the literature strictly as a null baseline, and make the
outcome-association the main evidence for what makes teamwork successful, with
explicit caution for n=38 and the 3-way split?

If you choose (C) or (A), do you also want me to keep the per-match
small-world comparison (option B's computation) as a *secondary* descriptive
result, or drop it entirely?

# Expert Question 3 — How to present the weak, partially counter-literature outcome associations as coach advice (sub-3) and generalization (sub-4)

## What the data shows (rounds 1–2 complete)

Structural baseline (honest, per your round-2 guidance):
- Season intra-team network: 30 nodes, 656 directed edges. Clustering 0.888 vs
  ER null 0.937 / degree-preserving CM null 0.904 → **not a clustering
  outlier**; APL 1.214 vs ER 1.063. So "dense, short-path, low-hub, weakly
  modular (modularity 0.068), small-world-adjacent."
- Per-match/per-half small-world comparison (secondary): mean real clustering
  0.719 vs ER 0.740 (diff −0.021, positive in only 36% of cases); APL real
  1.346 vs ER 1.263 (real longer in 99%). Clustering decays 1H→2H (0.776→0.662)
  while APL grows (1.260→1.433) — consistent with a fatigue/dispersal effect.

Outcome validation (n=38: 13 win / 10 tie / 15 loss; GD −14 overall):
| indicator | win mean | loss mean | Cohen d (win−loss) | r vs Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **bet_max** (top player betweenness) | 0.238 | 0.192 | **+0.76** | **+0.34 (p=.04)** |
| closeness_mean | 0.442 | 0.459 | −0.58 | −0.23 |
| mm_edges (M–M links) | 11.6 | 14.3 | −0.45 | −0.21 |
| cross_share | 0.011 | 0.015 | −0.43 | −0.20 |
| bet_gini (betweenness concentration) | 0.437 | 0.407 | +0.39 | +0.16 |

So the **one** outcome-associated indicator is: **winning matches have a more
concentrated hub (higher max betweenness, and higher betweenness Gini), fewer
midfield-midfield links, and fewer crosses** than losing matches. Everything
else (centroid, progress, pass entropy, clustering, pass count) is essentially
unassociated with outcome.

This is **weak** (a handful of n=38 correlations, the strongest p≈.04–.05,
multiple-comparison-prone) and **partly opposite** to the supplied literature
prior (Buldú et al. 2018: balanced betweenness, high closeness, forward centroid
→ better performance). Here centroid is not associated with outcome (r≈−0.02),
and *balanced* closeness/betweenness is associated with *loss*, not win.

Other context:
- Home/away: 10 of 13 wins at home, only 3 away (clear context effect).
- Coach change: Coach1 (matches 1–9) 2W/2T/5L; Coach3 (matches 15–38) 9W/7T/8L.
- Shots do **not** separate win from loss (win 9.15 vs loss 9.07 per match) —
  the gap is defensive/conversion, not shot volume.
- Substitutions: 3 per match, concentrated in M and F.

## Decision point

How should I write the coach-facing recommendations (sub-3) and the
generalization (sub-4) given these associations are weak and run opposite to
the prior?

- **Option A — "No robust structural lever; be cautious."**
  Report that no network indicator robustly predicts outcome at n=38; the
  bet_max signal is suggestive but not confirmed; therefore the honest
  recommendation is that structural changes are *not* clearly what separate
  wins from losses, and the coach should not over-rotate on network metrics.
  Generalization: team success in this sample is driven more by context

# Expert Question 1 — Scope of the teamwork model: which network scale and outcome target should anchor the analysis?

## Problem understanding

The 2020 MCM problem asks us (as "Intrepid Champion Modeling") to analyze last
season of a soccer team, the Huskies (38 matches, 19 opponents, 23,429 recorded
passes, 59,271 game events, 30 Huskies players). Four sub-questions:
(1) build passing networks and identify patterns from micro (dyads/triads) to
macro (whole network) scale and from minute-to-minute to season length;
(2) identify teamwork performance indicators *beyond points/wins* (diversity of
plays, coordination, distribution of contributions, tempo, etc.) and use them to
build a model of structural, configurational and dynamical teamwork, clarifying
whether strategies work universally or only against certain counter-strategies;
(3) advise the coach on structural strategies to change next season;
(4) generalize to how to design effective teams in society.

The literature we must apply (Buldú, Ferrer & Pastor-Satorras 2018, Front.
Psychol.) gives us: (a) small-world + heavy-tailed degree baseline for passing
networks, tested against null models; (b) betweenness/centrality and centroid
metrics correlate with win probability — so indicators must be validated against
match outcome.

## Decision point

There is one strategic fork that determines most of the downstream work — **which
network and which outcome anchor the core "teamwork model" of sub-question 2**:

- **Option A — Intra-team Huskies network + win/tie/loss:** build the directed
  weighted passing network *among the 30 Huskies players only* (their
  own-to-own passes) and test network indicators (clustering, path length,
  degree distribution, betweenness, centroid, triad census, pass-type entropy)
  against the 3-class match Outcome and goal difference. This is the
  most direct reading of "teamwork" — cooperation between teammates that produces
  success — and it uses the full 38-match outcome distribution.
- **Option B — Match joint network + goal margin:** build a joint Huskies+opponent
  network per match and relate it to the scoreline. Richer (captures interactions
  across teams) but mixes two different organizational units into one graph and
  makes "teamwork" less interpretable; the outcome target collapses to a single
  continuous margin per match.
- **Option C — Opponent-conditioned analysis only:** treat each opponent as a
  regime and build separate models per opponent. This directly answers
  "universally effective or counter-strategy-dependent" but fragments the sample
  (2 matches per opponent, n=38 total) to a point where most statistics are
  underpowered.

My inclination is **A as the primary model, with C as a secondary
robustness/context layer** (opponent-conditioned contrasts of the same
indicators, plus home/away and half-level splits), and B used only for a limited
purpose (e.g., measuring how often passes enter opponent territory via crosses
and forward progress, rather than modeling a joint graph).

## Why it matters

The choice fixes: which indicators enter the core model; what "validation"
means (3-class outcome vs. margin); how we use the small sample (n=38 matches);
and what the coach's actionable advice (sub-3) can legitimately claim. Getting
this wrong risks either an underpowered analysis or a model whose target is not
actually "teamwork."

## Candidate strategies

**Option A — Huskies-only intra-team network, outcome-validated.**
- Approach: aggregate Huskies→Huskies passes per match (and season), build
  dyad/triad census, null-model comparisons (Erdős–Rényi + degree-preserving
  Configuration Model + spatial null), centrality and entropy indicators, then
  correlate with Outcome/gd via effect sizes and a simple regularized classifier.
- Advantages: cleanest "teamwork" semantics; all 38 matches usable; indicators
  directly actionable for the coach; matches the literature baseline.
- Limitations: ignores opponent structure; with n=38 any per-opponent split is
  weak; 30 players → some players appear only in few matches (lineup changes).
- Expected impact: primary model + validation story for sub-questions 2–3.

**Option B — Joint match network.**
- Approach: nodes = all players in the match (10–22), edges = all recorded
  passes; model goal margin from joint network statistics.
- Advantages: captures cross-team interaction and transition passes.
- Limitations: mixes two teams' organization; "teamwork" indicator becomes
  muddled; opponent lineups vary, so the graph structure is driven partly by
  opponent identity rather than Huskies play.
- Expected impact: could be a secondary lens (territory/progress), but risky as
  the core model.

**Option C — Opponent-conditioned only.**
- Approach: separate indicators per opponent and per Side.
- Advantages: directly tests counter-strategy dependence.
- Limitations: n=2 matches per opponent → most contrasts are anecdotal;
  multiplicity across 19 opponents; cannot build a stable core model.
- Expected impact: useful only as a robustness/context layer, not the anchor.

**My recommended synthesis:** Option A anchors the core model; Option C runs as
an opponent/home–away/period conditioning layer on the *same* indicators; Option
B is reduced to territory/progress measures (e.g., x-progress of passes, share of
passes into the final third, crosses) used as supplementary indicators rather
than a joint graph.

## Question

Do you agree that the Huskies-only intra-team passing network, validated
against the 3-class match Outcome (with goal-difference as a secondary
continuous target), should anchor the core teamwork model — with
opponent/home–away/half-conditioned contrasts as a secondary robustness layer,
and joint match-graph analysis reduced to territory/progress measures? Or do you
prefer a different anchor (e.g., margin-anchored joint network), and if so, what
specific change to the anchor and to the validation target would you direct?

# Expert Question 2 — How to handle the (negative) small-world null-model result and the n=38 outcome validation

## Context from round 1

Per your direction, I anchored the core model on the Huskies-only intra-team
directed weighted passing network, validated against the 3-class Outcome (with
goal difference as secondary target), and reduced the joint graph to
territory/progress measures. I have now computed the season-level network
(n=30 players, 656 directed edges, aggregated over all 38 matches) and the
per-match feature table (38 rows).

## Empirical result that forces a strategic decision

The literature baseline (Buldú et al. 2018) says passing networks are
small-world: clustering well above the ER null, path length comparable to ER.
But my computed numbers do **not** show a clean small-world signature at the
season level:

| metric | Huskies real | ER null (n=30, m=656, mean of 50) | Degree-preserving CM null |
|---|---|---|---|
| average clustering | 0.888 | **0.937** | 0.904 |
| average path length | 1.214 | 1.063 | — |

Two issues:
1. With only 30 nodes and a dense graph (edge probability p≈0.74 in the ER null),
   the ER null is itself near-saturated, so its clustering is already ~0.94. The
   real network's clustering (0.888) is *slightly below* both nulls, and its path
   length (1.214) is *above* the ER null (1.063). So the standard "small-world"
   claim (clustering ≫ ER, APL ≈ ER) does **not** hold at season level — the
   network is dense and well-connected but not a clustering outlier.
2. At per-match level the graphs are sparser (~100 edges each), where the
   small-world comparison against a matched ER null is more meaningful, but
   still the absolute clustering is high and APL is short.

So there is a genuine tension: the external literature says "small-world," but
the data, with a properly matched (dense) null, does not show a clustering
outlier. The degree distribution also is not strongly heavy-tailed (out-degree
Gini ≈ 0.15, top hub M11 has betweenness 0.232 but most players have 25–30
out-links), and modularity is very low (0.068), i.e. weak community/formation
structure.

## Decision point

How should I frame and use the small-world / structural claim given that the
matched null-model result is *null* (not a significant outlier), and given the
constrained sample (n=38 matches, 3-class outcome with 13 win / 10 tie / 15 loss)?

- **Option A — Report the null honestly and re-anchor "success" on outcome-correlated indicators.**
  Present the null-model comparison accurately (clustering not an outlier, APL
  slightly longer than ER), conclude the season network is "dense and
  well-connected, hub-lite, weakly modular" rather than "small-world," and then
  lean on the per-match indicators that actually discriminate outcome
  (centroid_x, progress, betweenness balance, pass-type entropy, triad
  completion) for the coach-facing recommendations. This is statistically
  honest but drops the literature's small-world narrative.
- **Option B — Keep the small-world framing but move the comparison to the
  per-match / half scale where the matched null is less saturated.**
  Compute the small-world comparison (clustering vs. ER null, APL vs. ER null)
  *per match* (and per half), where the ER null is less near-saturated, report
  that the signature appears at the match scale (even if averaged out at season
  scale), and treat season-level as an aggregation that dilutes the signal.
  This preserves the literature narrative but risks over-claiming from a
  less-saturated null.
- **Option C — Hybrid: report both scales honestly, and use the outcome
  association (not the null-model novelty) as the main "what makes teamwork
  successful" evidence.** State clearly that the structural baseline is
  "dense, short-path, low-hub, weakly modular" (a small-world-adjacent regime
  but not a clustering outlier vs. matched null), and that the actionable
  insights come from which structural/territorial indicators correlate with
  wins vs. losses — with appropriate caution for n=38 and a 3-way outcome.

## Why it matters

The coach-facing recommendations (sub-3) and the generalized-team design
claims (sub-4) rest on which structural story I tell. If I over-claim
"small-world" the judge (who applied the literature) may credit the
narrative but I risk a statistical over-claim; if I drop it entirely I risk
not applying the provided external finding as instructed. The honest hybrid
(C) applies the literature as a *baseline to test against* (which is exactly
its intended use per external_data.md) while letting the data speak.

## Question

Given the matched-null result shows the season network is **not** a clustering
outlier (real 0.888 vs ER 0.937, CM 0.904) and is only weakly hub-dominated and
weakly modular, which framing do you direct for the submission:
(A) honest "not small-world, dense/well-connected" with success anchored purely
on outcome-correlated indicators;
(B) preserve the small-world narrative by moving the null-model comparison to
per-match / per-half scale;
or (C) the hybrid — report the baseline honestly as "dense, short-path,
low-hub, weakly modular (small-world-adjacent but not a clustering outlier vs
matched null)," apply the literature strictly as a null baseline, and make the
outcome-association the main evidence for what makes teamwork successful, with
explicit caution for n=38 and the 3-way split?

If you choose (C) or (A), do you also want me to keep the per-match
small-world comparison (option B's computation) as a *secondary* descriptive
result, or drop it entirely?

# Expert Question 1

## Problem Understanding

I am modeling the 2020_E plastic-waste problem for the International Council of
Plastic Waste Management (ICM). The four deliverables are:

1. A model estimating the **maximum level** of single-use / disposable plastic
   waste that can be **safely mitigated** without further environmental damage.
2. A discussion of **how far** waste can be reduced to reach an environmentally
   safe level, including regional policy effectiveness.
3. A target for the **minimum achievable level** of global single-use plastic
   waste, and its impacts.
4. A two-page memo to the ICM with a realistic target, timeline, and
   accelerators / hinders.

The two empirical anchors I have are:
- OECD (2022): 353 Mt waste in 2019; 33 Mt recycled (~9%); 460 Mt production;
  packaging is 40% of the waste stream; ~two-thirds of waste comes from
  plastics with useful life under 5 years.
- Jambeck et al. (2015): 4.8–12.7 MT/yr plastic entered the ocean in 2010
  (midpoint ≈ 8 MT/yr), from ~275 MT of coastal waste; mismanagement share
  ≈ 0.5–4.6% depending on region.

## Modeling Objective & Current Stage

I am about to formulate **Question 1**: a stock-and-flow (mass-balance) model
with a regional breakdown (high-income, middle-income, low-income coastal
regions), where:

- **Waste generated** = f(region, GDP, population, policy levers)
- **Waste flows** to: recycling, energy recovery, landfill, mismanaged
  (→ ocean leakage), and ambient
- **Mitigation capacity** = the maximum fraction of generated waste that can be
  processed by the existing resource base (recycling plants, energy-recovery
  facilities, collection infrastructure) without further environmental damage
- **Environmental damage** is benchmarked against the ocean-input threshold:
  keeping net new ocean input at or below the 2010 midpoint (~8 MT/yr) and
  drawing down the existing marine stock

## Unresolved Strategic Decision

**How should "safe mitigation capacity" be defined for Question 1?** I see two
candidate framings, and the choice has large downstream consequences for the
entire model:

**Option A — Throughput framing.** Safe mitigation capacity = the maximum
tonnage of single-use waste per year that existing (and near-term investable)
processing infrastructure can handle at a given quality-of-service level
(e.g. ≥ 90% capture, < 5% leakage), **independent of the ocean-input
threshold**. The ocean input is a *consequence* of the model, not the
definition of "safe." Safe = "we process it without it escaping into the
environment."

**Recommendation: Option C, with B binding.**

The problem asks for the maximum waste that can be mitigated "without further environmental damage." That clause is an outcome condition, not a throughput condition, so A alone answers a different question. But A is not discardable: infrastructure capacity is the physically achievable ceiling, and reporting it shows the ICM whether the binding constraint is engineering or ecological. C is therefore the honest framing.

On the parameters: 8 MT/yr is defensible only as a *reference* input, not a proven safe threshold — it is a historical midpoint, and Jambeck's own range spans 4.8–12.7. Use the lower bound (≈4.8 MT/yr) as the target and the midpoint as a sensitivity case. A 5%/yr drawdown is aggressive and hard to defend; prefer a slower, explicitly justified rate (1–2%/yr) or state drawdown qualitatively and let the ocean-input constraint bind.

**Recommendation: Option 3, and report the lever targets needed to make the floor durable.**

Option 1 hides the dip and ties the answer to an arbitrary horizon; Option 2 overstates a transient the system does not hold. The ICM asked for a *target* — a level to aim at and hold — so a durable level is the right object. The "sustained ≥10 years" convention is defensible: it is a stated reporting rule, not a hidden assumption, and any target must specify a holding period to be meaningful.

On the second question: report the lever targets that make the floor durable, not the floor of the current package. The creep-back to ~210 Mt/yr is a *finding*, not a nuisance — it says the current aggressive package is insufficient because population and consumption growth outrun it. The honest target is therefore stated as "hold ≈165–170 Mt/yr from ~2040 onward," with the additional levers (deeper source reduction, consumption caps, or continued recycling scaling) needed to prevent the rebound.

**Recommendation: Option C.**

A alone punishes low generators and leaves R3 with a target it cannot fund; B alone lets low capacity cap ambition precisely where impact is worst. C is the only framing that addresses both mismatches at once, and it gives the ICM a concrete instrument rather than a principle. It also matches the "common but differentiated responsibility" language the ICM's members already recognize, which makes it defensible as realistic.

**Single most important design feature: decouple R3's targets from its current capacity.**

The mechanism's purpose is to break the link between "what R3 can afford today" and "what R3 must achieve." If targets are set from present capacity, the fund merely subsidizes a low-ambition path and the impact mismatch persists. Grant-based finance and technology transfer are the *means*; decoupling is the *design principle* the memo should state first, with the fund and tech transfer presented as how it is operationalized.

**Recommendation: Option C, with B binding.**

The problem asks for the maximum waste that can be mitigated "without further environmental damage." That clause is an outcome condition, not a throughput condition, so A alone answers a different question. But A is not discardable: infrastructure capacity is the physically achievable ceiling, and reporting it shows the ICM whether the binding constraint is engineering or ecological. C is therefore the honest framing.

On the parameters: 8 MT/yr is defensible only as a *reference* input, not a proven safe threshold — it is a historical midpoint, and Jambeck's own range spans 4.8–12.7. Use the lower bound (≈4.8 MT/yr) as the target and the midpoint as a sensitivity case. A 5%/yr drawdown is aggressive and hard to defend; prefer a slower, explicitly justified rate (1–2%/yr) or state drawdown qualitatively and let the ocean-input constraint bind.

**Recommendation: Option 3, and report the lever targets needed to make the floor durable.**

Option 1 hides the dip and ties the answer to an arbitrary horizon; Option 2 overstates a transient the system does not hold. The ICM asked for a *target* — a level to aim at and hold — so a durable level is the right object. The "sustained ≥10 years" convention is defensible: it is a stated reporting rule, not a hidden assumption, and any target must specify a holding period to be meaningful.

On the second question: report the lever targets that make the floor durable, not the floor of the current package. The creep-back to ~210 Mt/yr is a *finding*, not a nuisance — it says the current aggressive package is insufficient because population and consumption growth outrun it. The honest target is therefore stated as "hold ≈165–170 Mt/yr from ~2040 onward," with the additional levers (deeper source reduction, consumption caps, or continued recycling scaling) needed to prevent the rebound.

**Recommendation: Option C.**

A alone punishes low generators and leaves R3 with a target it cannot fund; B alone lets low capacity cap ambition precisely where impact is worst. C is the only framing that addresses both mismatches at once, and it gives the ICM a concrete instrument rather than a principle. It also matches the "common but differentiated responsibility" language the ICM's members already recognize, which makes it defensible as realistic.

**Single most important design feature: decouple R3's targets from its current capacity.**

The mechanism's purpose is to break the link between "what R3 can afford today" and "what R3 must achieve." If targets are set from present capacity, the fund merely subsidizes a low-ambition path and the impact mismatch persists. Grant-based finance and technology transfer are the *means*; decoupling is the *design principle* the memo should state first, with the fund and tech transfer presented as how it is operationalized.

# Expert Question 1 — Strategic framing of the EDP modeling task

## Current understanding

The ICM-F wants a UN briefing that (1) quantifies the scope of environmentally
displaced persons (EDPs) — people at risk now and over time, plus the value of
the cultures at risk; (2) proposes international policies on EDP human rights
and cultural preservation; (3) presents a model measuring the impact of those
policies; (4) shows how the model was used to design/improve the policies; and
(5) argues, with the analysis, why the policies matter.

Empirical anchors available (pre-gathered, no further web searching): IPCC AR6
sea-level rise (0.38 m by 2100 SSP1-1.9, 0.56 m SSP2-4.5, 0.77 m SSP5-8.5,
~2 m tail); World Bank Groundswell 143 M internal climate migrants by 2050
(scale anchor; EDPs are the small cross-border/nationless subset); Pacific
atoll data — Kiribati/Marshall Islands/Tuvalu max elevation ~3 m, combined
~200,000 people, 0.5 m rise submerges 50–80% of urban areas; Maldives ~526,000
people, ~298 km².

## Current stage

Before building any model. The scope quantification, the cultural-value
measure, and the policy-impact model all depend on which overarching framing I
adopt, so I want the framing settled first.

## Decision point

How should I frame the core modeling question? The candidate framings are:

**A. Deterministic scenario timelines.** Pick the IPCC low/mid/high sea-level
scenarios and compute, per island nation, the year its habitable land falls
below a viability threshold (e.g., the 0.5 m / 50–80% urban-submergence
finding), giving a displacement date and EDP count per nation per scenario.
Clean, defensible, but hides deep uncertainty in the date.

**B. Probabilistic exposure model.** Model sea-level rise as a stochastic
process (uncertainty bands over the AR6 curves) and land viability as a
probabilistic threshold, yielding a probability distribution of displacement
time and expected-at-risk-population per nation, integrated over time to give
"people·years at risk." Richer but heavier and more assumptions.

**C. Two-tier hybrid (recommended).** Use A as the deterministic backbone
(scenario timelines and EDP counts per nation) and attach B's uncertainty
bands as a sensitivity overlay (earliest/latest displacement years, probability
that displacement occurs before a given year), without a full stochastic
integration. Balances rigor against the 3-expert budget.

Which framing do you endorse for this submission, and if a hybrid, should the
uncertainty overlay be scenario-based (discretized low/mid/high) or
probability-based (continuous distributions)?

## Why it matters

The framing dictates every downstream module: the scope estimate (point vs.
range of people at risk), the cultural-value loss trajectory (step function at
a displacement date vs. expected discounted loss), and the policy-impact
model (which needs a displacement-time input). Choosing B over A/C would
consume the expert budget and computation on stochastic machinery that may not
pay off for a UN-briefing deliverable; choosing A alone risks an over-precise
false certainty on the single most uncertain quantity in the whole problem.

# Expert Question 2 — Host-assignment obligation formula

## Current understanding

Per your round-1 endorsement, the submission uses the two-tier hybrid: a
deterministic displacement backbone (per-nation displacement year and EDP count
per IPCC low/mid/high scenario, viability threshold at 50% habitable land,
calibrated to the 0.5 m / 50–80% urban-submergence anchor) plus a discretized
scenario uncertainty overlay. The scope module places the four at-risk nations
(Tuvalu, Kiribati, Marshall Islands, Maldives; ~710k people in 2026, growing to
~1.2–1.3 M by 2100) on displacement timelines from ~2068 (Tuvalu, high scenario)
to ~2148 (Marshall Islands, low), and the tail (~2 m) stress test pushes all
four before 2046. The cultural-value module values each nation's cultural stock
(a lifetime per-person value of shared cultural experience, weighted by a
composite cultural-capital index) and tracks its discounted loss.

## Current stage

Module 3 (policy impact). The next strategic choice is how the model allocates
the EDP cohorts to host countries — the answer to "what countries will take
them."

## Decision point

The problem explicitly asks whether "the worst offenders" (disproportionate
historical and current greenhouse-gas contributions) should carry a higher
obligation. My candidate obligation formulas:

**A. Capacity-proportional (pure).** Each host's share of total EDPs is
proportional to its population/capacity share only. Simple, but ignores the
emission-responsibility question entirely, which the problem names directly.

**B. Responsibility-adjusted capacity (recommended).** share = capacity_share
× responsibility_factor, where the factor is 1.0 for regional neighbors, 1.15
for major emitters, 1.25 for colonial-historical powers (UK, France), and 1.30
for historical emitters (USA). This bakes the "worst offenders owe more"
principle into the allocation as a bounded multiplier rather than a free
variable, keeping every host's share in a defensible 5–19% band.

**C. Full historical-emission accounting.** Weight each host by its actual
cumulative historical + current per-capita GHG emissions (e.g., USA/UK/EU
dominate). Most "principled" on the emissions question, but it would assign
enormous shares to a few rich emitters, concentrate the whole Maldivian
cohort in the US/EU, and produce numbers that look punitive and politically
unworkable in a UN-briefing context.

Which do you endorse for the host-assignment module, and — if B — is a bounded
multiplier (1.0–1.3) the right way to express "higher obligation," or should
the responsibility factor be a single uniform premium applied to all
emitting/colonial hosts?

## Why it matters

This is the module that operationalizes the problem's central normative
question. The choice changes (i) which countries the briefing names as the
principal obligors, (ii) whether the Maldives' large cohort is concentrated in
one or spread across many hosts (with direct consequences for the
cluster-based cultural-preservation policy I am building), and (iii) whether
the recommendation reads as a defensible UN treaty formula or as an
unworkable punitive quota. It also feeds the cluster-settlement dynamics, since
cohort concentration per host determines the cultural-retention input.

# Expert Question 3 — Governance and decision rights in the EDP resettlement treaty

## Current understanding

Per your round-1 endorsement the submission uses the two-tier hybrid (deterministic
displacement backbone per IPCC low/mid/high scenario, with a discretized scenario
uncertainty overlay), and per your round-2 endorsement the host-assignment module
uses responsibility-adjusted capacity: each host's share is its capacity share
times a bounded tiered multiplier (1.0 regional, 1.15 major emitter, 1.25
colonial-historical, 1.30 historical emitter), with a 60/40 split of each cohort
between its regional cluster hosts and the top global obligors. End-2026
obligation shares fall in a 5–19% band (USA 18.9%, Australia 16.1%, Fiji 12.9%,
Germany/Japan ~9.3%, UK 8.1%). The policy-impact model compares three regimes —
do-nothing, rights-only, rights + cultural protection — and the final package
couples guaranteed EDP asylum with fast-tracked citizenship and a funded
cluster-based cultural-protection rider.

## Current stage

Module 4 (recommendation to the UN). The last strategic choice is the
governance question the problem names explicitly: who gets a say in deciding
where these nationless EDPs make a new home.

## Decision point

**A. Individual-centric.** Displacement status and preferred destination are
determined by each person's (or family's) consent and choice, with the UN
administering a claims process. Strongest on the rights side, but host
governments may reject an obligation formula they did not co-author, and it
offers no mechanism to enforce the proportional-obligation shares.

**B. UN-centralized (recommended).** The UN runs an intergovernmental treaty
body that (i) certifies a nation's viability against the model's threshold,
(ii) assigns cohorts to hosts using the responsibility-adjusted formula, and
(iii) adjudicates disputes — while the EDPs retain veto and
relocation-preference rights within the assignment (they consent to the cohort
destination and may request an alternative host from their obligation list).
This gives the obligation formula its enforcement mechanism and keeps EDP
agency inside a bounded process.

**C. Host-governance-led.** Each receiving state sets its own intake rules and
the EDPs negotiate bilaterally; the UN only brokers. Most politically
realistic in the short run, but it reproduces the asymmetry the model exists
to correct: hosts with the largest responsibility-adjusted shares (USA, UK,
Germany, Japan) would have the least incentive to accept them, and the
cluster-size minimums needed for cultural retention would not be guaranteed.

Which governance arrangement do you endorse for the UN briefing, and if B — is
granting EDPs a veto on their cohort's destination the right calibration of
"individual voice" within a UN-centralized process, or should their role be
advisory only (no veto), given that a veto could be used to stall an
otherwise-consistent assignment?

## Why it matters

This is the module that turns the model's outputs into a recommendation the UN
can actually adopt. The choice determines (i) whether the proportional-obligation
formula is enforceable or aspirational, (ii) whether the cluster-settlement
minimums the cultural-preservation policy depends on can be guaranteed, and
(iii) how the briefing answers the problem's final question — individuals vs.
UN vs. host governments — which the judge will read as the submission's
normative conclusion.
expert_answers:
Endorse **C, the two-tier hybrid**, with a **scenario-based (discretized low/mid/high) uncertainty overlay**, not a continuous probabilistic one.

Rationale: the UN-briefing deliverable needs defensible, communicable numbers, and the displacement date is the problem's most uncertain quantity. A gives the clean backbone (per-nation displacement year and EDP count per scenario); the discretized overlay supplies earliest/latest years and "probability displacement occurs before year Y" without the stochastic-integration cost. Discretized scenarios align with the IPCC anchors already in hand, keep the cultural-loss trajectory interpretable as a step function with bracketed timing, and feed the policy-impact model a bounded displacement-time input. A full probabilistic model (B) would spend the expert budget on machinery whose added precision the underlying sea-level and viability assumptions cannot support.

Endorse **B, responsibility-adjusted capacity**, with a **bounded, tiered multiplier (1.0–1.3)**, not a single uniform premium.

Rationale: the problem names the "worst offenders" question directly, so a pure capacity formula (A) would visibly dodge a required normative commitment. But full historical-emission accounting (C) converts the allocation into a punitive quota that concentrates cohorts and undermines the cluster-based cultural-preservation policy downstream. A bounded tiered multiplier keeps the "higher obligation" principle explicit and auditable while preserving the 5–19% share band and cohort dispersion.

Tiering (rather than one uniform premium) is correct because the problem distinguishes *historical* from *current* contributions and colonial-historical ties; collapsing these into a single premium discards that distinction and weakens the briefing's defensibility. Keep the tiers few, transparent, and justified in one sentence each.

Endorse **B, UN-centralized**, with EDPs holding a **bounded veto** — not advisory-only.

Rationale: the problem asks who decides, and only a UN treaty body can enforce the responsibility-adjusted obligation shares and guarantee the cluster-size minimums the cultural-preservation rider depends on. Host-led governance (C) reproduces the asymmetry the model corrects; individual-centric (A) leaves the formula unenforceable.

On calibration: give EDPs a veto over their *cohort's destination* and a right to request an alternative host from their obligation list — but bound it. A veto that can stall an otherwise-consistent assignment indefinitely defeats the enforcement mechanism. Calibrate it as a **one-time, time-limited objection** (e.g., a single alternative-host request, adjudicated by the treaty body within a fixed window), so individual voice is real but cannot be used to block the system. Advisory-only would hollow out the rights commitment the briefing rests on; unbounded veto would hollow out the formula. The bounded veto is the defensible middle.
